2020-1-1:
An EXCEPT question: three options are argued in the passage, one is not.

  • A: the revolution ended with the new class of politicians re-establishing central state power, betraying workers and peasants. Argued.
  • B: the passage says the new rulers applied “violence and terror, a secret police, and a professional army”, and that for anarchists the state itself is the enemy. Argued.
  • C: individualist anarchism has several traditions (Stirner, the American thinkers), all stressing individual autonomy. Argued.
  • D: the passage notes that “anarchy” was once a derogatory word, but never says why, and never links the popular image of lawlessness to mistrust of collectivism. Not argued.

So the answer is D.
2020-1-2:
We need the explanation that fits the anarchists’ account of revolutions.

The passage says workers and peasants seized the chance to end exploitation, yet were “betrayed by the new class of politicians”, who then used violence, secret police and an army to keep control.

Option D matches this: the new rulers rose on the workers’ anger and then oppressed them.

  • A: the rulers were not anarchists; anarchists oppose any state.
  • B: nothing suggests anarchists were too weak; the betrayal is by the politicians.
  • C: a power-sharing deal with the old elite is not mentioned.

So the answer is D.
2020-1-3:
The last sentence says the American individualists protect their own autonomy but also stress “associating with others for common advantages”, and differ from free-market liberals in their “emphasis on mutualism” and mistrust of capitalism.

So both value individual autonomy, but only the former add mutual dependence. That is option A.

  • B: the American thinkers are not said to favour a people’s state.
  • C: they distrust capitalism absolutely, so no argument for a “morally upright capitalism”.
  • D: altruism and a “mystical” market are not in the passage.

So the answer is A.
2020-1-4:
The passage is about anarchism, its hostility to the state, and the individual and communal freedom it defends.

Option A (Anarchism, State, Individual, Freedom) covers exactly these.

  • B: strikes are never discussed.
  • C: “protection” and liberals are side points.
  • D: betrayal and power belong to one part of the argument, and individual freedom, which both anarchist-communism and individualism stress, is missing.

So the answer is A.
2020-1-5:
Whatever the variety, anarchism rejects centralised authority. Anarchist-communism opposes “any central authority”, the historical argument makes “the state itself” the enemy, and even the individualists want free association rather than rule.

Option B states this common thread.

  • A: Proudhon only adopted the word; not all forms derive from him.
  • C: anarchist-communism puts communities, not the individual, first.
  • D: the passage does identify a shared idea, so denying it is wrong.

So the answer is B.
2020-1-6:
The passage says coins suited small transactions, and that textiles lost value when cut: cutting a bolt “greatly lessened the value”.

A one-eighth purchase can be paid in coins, in grain, or with a worn piece of cloth of about the same value. Cutting an eighth off a new bolt wastes value, so it is the unsound choice.

  • A: grain was an accepted currency, so an appropriate weight works.
  • B: a faded bolt is worth less than a new one, so one of equal value fits.
  • C: coins were meant for small, local transactions.

So the answer is D.
2020-1-7:
Check what “steady” and “stable” describe: the bolt’s dimensions (56 cm by 12 m) stayed constant, which means reliable measurement; textile values were more stable than coin values, which means reliable quality and value; textile supply had fewer problems, which means reliable supply.

Transportation is mentioned only in terms of weight, not steadiness, so A is the exception.

So the answer is A.
2020-1-8:
The closing paragraph compares the Tang system with ours: coins for small payments, notes and other instruments for larger ones, and a system in flux. This supports D.

  • A: nothing says deteriorating currency was barred from official use; grain, which rots, was used for taxes and salaries.
  • B: coins were not shown to be more valuable or durable than textiles.
  • C: grain was used less than coins and textiles.

So the answer is D.
2020-1-9:
The passage draws parallels: several forms of money (coins, notes, cards versus coins, cloth, grain), different forms for small and large payments, and a system that is changing “in front of our eyes”.

Nothing says the Tang system was itself being transformed; the passage presents it as an established system with several currencies. So “undergoing transformation” is the feature not shared.

So the answer is D.
2020-1-10:
We need the statement that is false but whose falsity backs the author.

The author says complete sentences need a noun (subject) and a verb (predicate). So “Perish the thought that complete sentences necessarily need nouns and verbs” is false, and if it is false the author is right that they do need them.

  • A: true, and it states the argument, so it does not fit the “false” condition.
  • B: unrelated to the passage.
  • C: true, quoted from Strunk.

So the answer is D.
2020-1-11:
The author’s claim is that any noun plus any verb makes a sentence: a minimal ingredient, then a result.

Option A has the same shape (any vegetable plus some spices gives a dish). In B, an apple tree planted in a field does not automatically make an orchard, since one tree is not an orchard. C is wrong because nouns alone make no sentence. D is wrong because shared equipment does not make a team.

So the answer is A.
2020-1-12:
The passage opens with the need for agreed grammar rules and warns that “when these rules break down, confusion and misunderstanding result”. The rest is about grasping the basics so that one writes well.

The best single line for this concern is “Bad grammar produces bad sentences.”

  • A: a supporting point about Strunk’s remark.
  • C: a detail about simple sentences.
  • D: only one part of the argument (nouns and verbs).

So the answer is B.
2020-1-13:
An EXCEPT question.

  • A: the author says you need not write complete sentences every time. Inferable.
  • B: noun is subject and verb is predicate, by definition. Inferable.
  • C: grammar is not said to exist to keep sentences simple; simple sentences are only a “safety net”. Not inferable.
  • D: the Grammar Police are a joking image for rule enforcers. Inferable.

So the answer is C.
2020-1-14:
The author values knowing the rules of grammar and thinks they help a writer judge her own work.

Language software that standardises the rules as an aid to writers fits this. The others clash: B calls for breaking rules, C avoids rhetoric (the author does not reject it), and D attacks standard rules.

So the answer is A.
2020-1-15:
An EXCEPT question about what Le Boeuf’s study supports.

  • A: dialects arose after recolonisation from one small surviving herd. Supported.
  • B: individual pulse stayed the same through life while the average changed. Supported.
  • C: the calls were expected to regress towards the founder colony’s average, so Año Nuevo would not exceed Isla Guadalupe. Not supported.
  • D: the average rose from 1968 to 1972 and dialects later vanished, which implies a rise. Supported.

So the answer is C.
2020-1-16:
Dialects disappeared because immigrants’ faster calls pulled the host average towards the founder’s average. To keep dialects, each colony’s average would have had to stay distinct.

If immigrants changed their tempo to match the residents, the host colony’s average would not shift, so the difference would persist. That is D.

  • A: a colony with no migration changes nothing in the other colonies.
  • B: hosts changing to match immigrants would speed up the homogenising.
  • C: a second founder with the same average would not stop mixing.

So the answer is D.
2020-1-17:
The passage says the 1960s calls were “quite simple”, with dialects as only a tempo change. Today’s males show “more individual diversity”, more complex calls, and the regional dialects have vanished.

So simple, less individual variety, great regional variety became complex, great individual variety, less regional variety, which is B.

  • A: covers only pulse rates, not the full transformation.
  • C and D reverse one or more of these trends.

So the answer is B.
2020-1-18:
The southern rookeries were recolonised from Isla Guadalupe. The passage explains faster rates elsewhere by chance: seals with faster rates “would have happened to arrive first”.

So the faster-calling Guadalupe seals may have been the original settlers of the southern rookeries, option A.

  • B: the southern seals migrating to Año Nuevo is the effect described, not the cause.
  • C: the direction is reversed.
  • D: complex structures are a modern feature, not tied to the southern rookeries.

So the answer is A.
2020-1-19:
The paragraph is about how feminists approach reading. Order: 1 (how we read is linked to what we read), then 5 (“more specifically”, the canon is androcentric and harms women readers), then 4 (documenting “this realization” was an early task), then 2 (Showalter’s critique as an example of that work).

Sentence 3 is a general claim about how androcentric literature shapes reading by gender. It does not link to sentences 5 and 4 by their “this realization” chain, so it is the odd one.

So the answer is 3.
2020-1-20:
The passage sets out the old view of intelligence (inborn, single, fixed, measurable), then says biologists doubt both that “intelligence” is one coherent entity and that heritability can be estimated in humans.

Option A captures both biological criticisms in the final sentence, the single-entity doubt and the doubt about estimating heritability.

  • B: covers only the first doubt and says “criticised the conventional wisdom” too broadly.
  • C: shifts the criticism to psychologists’ view of immutability, which the passage does not attribute to biologists.
  • D: the option is cut off and does not complete the heritability point.

So the answer is A.
2020-1-21:
Sentence 1 states the problem: narrative structure alone cannot reveal the meaning of San folktales. Sentence 4 gives the remedy (probing words and phrases in original-language records). Sentence 3 reports what the selected tales then reveal (spiritual conflict involving malevolent shamans), and 2 follows with what benign shamans do in response.

So the order is 1, 4, 3, 2. The pair 1 then 4 (problem, then method) is the anchor.

So the answer is 1432.
2020-1-22:
The passage traces Europe changing its structure each century and now setting aside its old political mechanisms to adopt a common currency and a formal political structure, in response to a multipolar world and German unification.

D captures this last step, the move towards a common currency and political structure to adapt to the multipolar world.

  • A and C stress a consistent adaptation story in general terms; the passage’s point is the current unification.
  • B names a cause (Germany plus multipolarity) but misses the common currency and the break from earlier mechanisms.

So the answer is D.
2020-1-23:
The passage says films like Clear and Present Danger give a false picture of forensic phonetics, leading to the “CSI effect”: unrealistic expectations of what the science can do.

Option C expresses this, that screen portrayals make the technique seem robust and fool-proof.

  • A: the passage is about expectations, not the science’s base being shaky.
  • B: it says the film’s method is unrealistic, not that it is used in real life.
  • D: the passage does not say voice recognition has become prominent because of the media.

So the answer is C.
2020-1-24:
Sentence 3 opens with the time frame and the general claim (continuity and change since the 1990s). Sentence 1 gives the first example, ongoing tensions among the 11 states. Sentence 2 adds China’s rise as a new concern, and sentence 4 (“These concerns”) shows outsiders taking interest.

Sentence 4 must follow 2, since “these concerns” points back to it.

So the answer is 3124.
2020-1-25:
The paragraph is about slave talk as a form of agency. Order: 4 (speech was a white privilege, but slavery depended on dialogue), then 1 (talk was the commonest way to subvert), then 2 (even in extreme violence, words stayed irrepressible), then 5 (owners obsessed over and feared slave talk).

Sentence 3, about the African origins of oaths and invocations, is about the cultural roots of speech, not about its use under slavery, so it breaks the thread.

So the answer is 3.
2020-1-26:
Sentence 1 starts with poisons used in war since early civilisation. Sentence 3 brings in microbiology and biological weapons, and sentence 2 follows with “These dangers”, referring to those new prospects, and the declarations of 1874 and 1899. Sentence 4 comes last, noting that the treaties lacked any means of control.

Sentence 2 must come after 3, because “These dangers” needs a prior mention of the new weapons.

So the answer is 1324.
